title: Applying the business case: canvas, value, MVP and personas
blurb: Apply the business case practice in a scenario: the right product for each piece of information, value focus, the MVP, the develop, check, maintain, confirm cycle and personas.
question: At Larkspur Rail, Release 1 of Fair Fares is the minimum viable product and must be live by the end of month four. What should the project canvas say about it, and why?

teach.h: Tailor the business case, never drop it
teach.body: Every project needs business justification. In PRINCE2 Agile the business case keeps its purpose (is the project desirable, viable and achievable?) but is usually tailored into a project canvas: a one-page visual case built from estimated costs against expected benefits and value, offset by risks. Three more products support it: the project brief, the benefits management approach and the sustainability management approach.

head: Product or artifact
In an agile project it holds
rows: Flexible areas of scope and quality criteria; agile techniques chosen and why; impact on operations
Costs against benefits and value, offset by risks; identifies the MVP
Benefits actions and reviews; frequent releases for early benefits
Actions, reviews and controls for sustainability targets
teach.caption: The sustainability management approach is the PRINCE2 7 product carried into agile; Table 3.1 fixes sustainability at its minimum criteria.

teach.h: The eight elements of a project canvas
teach.caption: The canvas should also outline best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios (Table 5.2).

teach.h: Focus on value, prove it early with an MVP
teach.body: Every effort should contribute to meaningful outcomes for users and stakeholders, so work that solves real problems comes first. A practical way is to give each user story a value and prioritize by value to the objective. An MVP tests core features or key assumptions with minimal investment. If one is used, the canvas must identify it, so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late.

steps.label: Develop
steps.sub: Explore options; get information for investment decisions

steps.label: Maintain
steps.sub: Keep it up to date (PRINCE2 step)

steps.label: Confirm
steps.sub: Have benefits been, or will they be, realized?

teach.caption: Confirming benefits mostly happens after closure, but iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project (6.3.1).
A plan, report or feature is an output, never a benefit (Glossary, Figure 6.3).

items: Use them to identify and articulate specific benefits for users, customers and stakeholders.
Write them in a cross-functional workshop that includes development team members.
Keep them fictional: the abstraction leaves more room for innovation.
Base them on user needs, not demographics such as age, occupation or income.
For an agile pilot or new product, write no more than five.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Larkspur Rail, Fair Fares
teach.body: Commercial director Bronwen Hale leads the project canvas. Benefits: the share of eligible app journeys compensated automatically, with a tolerance, against the 80% contract threshold. Scope: the three releases as epics. The canvas names Release 1 as the MVP so the board hears early if it slips. The benefits management approach plans frequent releases so compensation reaches passengers before closure, and the sustainability management approach covers the carbon-saved target.

teach.text: Three classic traps: dropping the business case because the team is agile (tailor it instead); listing an output such as a plan or feature as a benefit; and building personas from demographics or real named people instead of fictional, needs-based users.

items: Project canvas: vision, business value, options, costs, users, scope, benefits, major risks.
Identify the MVP in the canvas so a late MVP can trigger an exception.
Project brief: flexible scope and quality areas and the agile techniques chosen.
Benefits management approach: reviews, measures, frequent releases for early benefits.
Develop, check, maintain, confirm; personas are fictional, needs-based, at most five for pilots.

summary: You can now put each piece of business case information in the right product, apply value focus and the MVP, and name the business case technique step in use. You can also judge whether personas are written the PRINCE2 Agile way.

A.q: Bronwen Hale is drafting the project canvas for Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project. Release 1, the minimum viable product, must be live by the end of month four. What should the canvas do about the MVP?
options: Leave it to the release map so the canvas stays short
Identify it, so an exception can be raised if it is late
List its user stories with their acceptance criteria
Record it as the main measurable benefit of the project
A.why: If an MVP is used, the project canvas must identify it so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be delivered late (Table 6.1, 6.3.1).

whyNot.0: The release map shows releases and timing, but the canvas itself must identify the MVP.
whyNot.2: User stories and acceptance criteria belong in the backlogs, not in the one-page canvas.
whyNot.3: The MVP is a product, an output; benefits are measurable improvements.

A.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team wants personas for the online carers' self-assessment, its first agile product. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on personas?
options: Base each persona on a named carer from the network
Group carers by age, income and occupation first
Have the user researcher write them, then send them to the team
Write a few fictional, needs-based personas in a team workshop
A.why: Personas should be written in a cross-functional workshop with development team members, kept fictional, based on user needs rather than demographics, and limited to five for a new product or pilot (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Personas should be fictional; the abstraction widens the range for innovation.
whyNot.1: Demographics such as age, occupation and income no longer predict shared needs; personas are needs-based.
whyNot.2: Personas should be written in a cross-functional workshop with the developers, which builds collaboration and identification with users.

A.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team has a long list of user stories for the repairs journey. Service design lead Raj Malhotra wants to apply the business case guidance on focusing on value. What should he do?
options: Give each story a value and prioritize by value to the objective
Order the stories by estimated effort, with the smallest first
Deliver the stories in the order the tenants first raised them
Wait for the full business case before ordering any stories
A.why: Focus on value means each effort contributes to meaningful outcomes; in practice, assign a value to each user story and prioritize by its value to the objective (6.3.1).

whyNot.1: Effort matters for planning, but ordering by size does not focus the work on value.
whyNot.2: The order requests arrived in says nothing about their value to the objective.
whyNot.3: Value-based prioritization is done continuously; waiting for a detailed case delays the most valuable work.

B.q: Larkspur Rail wants passengers to receive compensation before the project ends. The project manager must describe how benefits will be measured and reviewed, and that frequent releases are planned for early benefits. Where should this go?
options: Project brief
Benefits management approach
Project canvas
Sustainability management approach
B.why: The benefits management approach defines benefits management actions and reviews, including measurement and tolerance guidance; in agile, frequent releases are planned there to enable early delivery of benefits (Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: The project brief outlines flexible scope and quality areas and chosen techniques, not the benefits review procedure.
whyNot.2: The canvas lists the expected, measurable benefits and their tolerance, but not how they will be reviewed.
whyNot.3: The sustainability management approach covers sustainability targets, not the general benefits reviews.

B.q: During starting up at Pinewick Home and Garden, project manager Patrick Dunne drafts the project brief. Delivery will be incremental across the website and 85 stores. What should the brief include for an agile project?
options: A detailed task plan for each team's two-week sprint
The full set of user stories with their story points
Flexible scope and quality areas and agile techniques
The team skill matrix for every delivery team
B.why: In agile, the project brief outlines the flexible areas of scope and quality criteria based on prioritization, the agile techniques chosen and their expected benefits, and more detail on the impact on operations (Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: Task-level plans are team plans for the next iteration, made in managing product delivery.
whyNot.1: User stories and estimates sit in the backlogs, not the brief.
whyNot.3: The team skill matrix is an organization technique completed in the project kickoff workshop.

B.q: In starting up at Larkspur Rail, Bronwen's team compares three options (full in-app compensation, a website form only, and doing the minimum) and gathers cost and benefit data before the board decides to invest. Which step of the business case technique is this?
options: Confirm
Check
Maintain
Develop
B.why: Develop means exploring options and getting the right information on which investment decisions can be made (6.3.1, Figure 6.3).

whyNot.0: Confirm assesses whether intended benefits have been or will be realized, mostly after closure.
whyNot.1: Check assesses whether a project is (still) worthwhile once a case exists; here the case is being built.
whyNot.2: Maintain keeps an existing business case up to date; no case exists yet.

C.q: Draycott's operations director says Release 1 on ten machines is the minimum that would justify continuing. The project manager writes 'lower breakdown costs on the ten machines, with tolerance' under benefits in the canvas and 'sensors on ten machines' under scope. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because a benefit is a measurable improvement, not an output
Yes, because the canvas should list every feature as a user story
No, because benefits are mostly confirmed after the project closes
No, because minimum viability of benefits can be flexed downwards
C.why: Benefits are measurable improvements from an outcome; fitted sensors are an output, which belongs under scope (project product, epics). Separating them is right (Glossary, 6.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: The canvas is a one-page view; it does not list every user story.
whyNot.2: True of the confirm step, but it does not make listing measurable benefits in the canvas wrong.
whyNot.3: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability and flexed only above it (Table 3.1).

C.q: Saltmarsh's project manager proposes dropping the business case because the team works in two-week iterations and the backlog already shows what matters. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because agile replaces the business case with the backlog
Yes, because a value is assigned to each user story instead
No, because justification is still needed, for example a canvas
No, because the CPO should own the business case instead
C.why: All projects must have business justification. PRINCE2 Agile tailors the business case, typically into a project canvas, rather than removing it (6.3.1, Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: The backlog lists requirements; it does not document costs against benefits offset by risks.
whyNot.1: Valuing stories supports prioritization, but it does not justify the investment as a whole.
whyNot.3: The project executive leads the project canvas; the CPO owns the project backlog, not the business case.

C.q: Callowmere's web team, new to personas, writes nine personas for the Student Support Hub, a new product being piloted with agile ways of working. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because more personas widen the range for innovation
Yes, because personas help identify benefits for users
No, because the student design panel should write them
No, because a pilot or new product needs no more than five
C.why: For agile pilots or new products, PRINCE2 Agile advises no more than five personas; more are possible only at high agile maturity, as too many shift focus and make prioritizing harder (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Innovation comes from keeping personas fictional, not from having many of them.
whyNot.1: True, but it does not justify nine personas for a pilot.
whyNot.2: Personas should be co-written in a cross-functional workshop with development team members.

reteach.title: The one-page pitch
reteach.question: If you had one page to convince a funder, what would you put on it?

blocks.h: Think of the canvas as a pitch
blocks.body: A funder wants to know where you are heading (vision), why it matters (business value), what else you considered (options), what it costs, who it is for (users), what you will build (scope), what will measurably improve (benefits) and what could go wrong (major risks). That is the project canvas. The first small thing you release to learn fast is the MVP, and the canvas names it so a delay is spotted.

blocks.text: A feature, plan or report is what you build (scope). A benefit is the measurable improvement it leads to.

explain.body: Project brief: flexible scope and quality areas and chosen agile techniques. Project canvas: the justification. Benefits management approach: benefits actions, reviews and frequent releases. Sustainability management approach: actions, reviews and controls for sustainability targets.

test.q: Larkspur Rail must define the actions, reviews and controls for its target of moving journeys from car to rail, including the carbon-saved figure in the alerts. Which product should hold this?
options: Benefits management approach
Sustainability management approach
Project brief
Communication management approach
test.why: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls to achieve the project's sustainability performance targets (PRINCE2 7 product carried into agile).

whyNot.0: The benefits approach handles benefits reviews, not sustainability targets.
whyNot.2: The brief outlines flexible scope and chosen techniques, not sustainability controls.
whyNot.3: The communication approach covers how and how often information flows to and from stakeholders.

explain.body: Prioritize by value to the objective. An MVP is a basic version built with minimal cost and time to test core features and assumptions and gather early feedback. It is not the finished product.

test.q: Easterholm releases a basic carers' self-assessment first, with minimal investment, to test its core features with the carers' network before building more. What is Release 1 acting as?
options: A minimum viable product
A risk-adjusted backlog
A benefits review
A stage tolerance
test.why: An MVP is a basic version built with minimal cost and time to test core features and gather early feedback (6.3.1).

whyNot.1: A risk-adjusted backlog holds stories and risk responses together; it is not a release.
whyNot.2: A benefits review measures realized benefits; this is a product release.
whyNot.3: A tolerance is a permitted deviation, not a product.

explain.body: Develop the case by exploring options; check whether it is still worthwhile; maintain it as the project goes; confirm whether benefits have been or will be realized. Confirmation mostly follows closure.

test.q: A year after Saltmarsh's Repairs Reimagined project closes, the board measures whether second visits fell as the canvas expected. Which business case technique step is this?
options: Develop
Check
Confirm
Maintain
test.why: Confirm assesses whether the intended benefits have been or will be realized; it mostly takes place after closure (6.3.1).

whyNot.1: Check asks whether the project is still worthwhile during the project.
whyNot.3: Maintain keeps the case current while the project runs; it has closed.

explain.body: Fictional users built around needs, written in a cross-functional workshop with developers, no more than five for a pilot or new product. They help articulate specific benefits for users.

test.q: Draycott's software team is writing personas for the maintenance dashboard. Which basis should the personas use?
options: Each engineer's age and years of service
The real names of the senior engineers
What engineers need to know before a failure
The job grades used in the pay structure
test.why: Personas are based on user needs, not demographics, and are kept fictional (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Age and service length are demographics, which no longer predict shared needs.
whyNot.1: Personas should be fictional, not real named people.
whyNot.3: Job grades are an occupational grouping, not user needs.
